query: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its deformation behavior remains poorly understood. Under mechanical-property and deformation testing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this low hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison, predict the observations relative to the starting state, state the applicable composition, structural-state, and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to the reported property combination, and specify a falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Grain refinement in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy will obstruct dislocation glide and enhance strain hardening, resulting in increased hardness and yield strength compared to its coarse-grained, as‐cast state. This implies that the alloy’s low hardness and strength are primarily due to facile dislocation motion in the coarse microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or near‐equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a coarse-grained, single-phase solid solution with low dislocation barrier density
generation.intervention: Thermomechanical processing (cold working followed by controlled annealing) to produce a refined-grained microstructure while keeping the composition and phase unchanged
generation.conditions: Testing at ambient temperature under controlled strain-rate deformation conditions; the composition is maintained as equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state without additional precipitates
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction in grain size increases the density of grain boundaries, which in turn act as obstacles to dislocation motion and promote dislocation storage for strain hardening
generation.mechanism: In the coarse-grained state, dislocations can glide easily with minimal interactions, leading to low hardness and strength. Grain refinement increases dislocation barrier density, enhances strain hardening, and thus raises the yield strength and hardness
generation.predicted_outcome: Refined-grained samples will exhibit significantly higher Vickers hardness and yield strength compared to the as-cast coarse-grained samples under identical loading conditions
generation.baseline: The as-cast, coarse-grained equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy with favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength
generation.boundary: The applied hypothesis is valid as long as the alloy remains in a single-phase solid solution and is deformed at ambient conditions with typical strain rates; no other microstructural phases or precipitates form during processing
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement is uncertain, and other factors such as residual stresses or solute segregation effects might also influence the observed mechanical properties

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy samples. Set A will be maintained in the as-cast, coarse-grained state. Set B will undergo controlled thermomechanical processing (cold deformation followed by annealing) to yield a refined-grained microstructure. Both sets will be subjected to identical ambient temperature compression/tensile tests.
measurements: Yield strength determination via stress-strain curves
Microstructural characterization (grain size analysis) using microscopy techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined-grained samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength compared to the as-cast samples, or if the microstructural analysis shows no substantial grain refinement, then the hypothesis that facile dislocation glide due to coarse grains governs the low hardness and strength would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Concurrent strength–ductility improvement of HfMoTaTiZr is achieved via Cr addition and the underlying strengthening mechanism was discussed. 4.2 at% Cr addition into HfMoTaTiZr led to the formation of a Laves phase, in addition to the BCC phase. The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 is 535.8 Hv 0.3 , 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr. The yield strength and fracture strain of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 reach 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa and 14.0 ± 2.9%, respectively, 207.5 MPa and 20.6% higher than HfMoTaTiZr. Solid solution hardening and the presence of the intermetallic Laves phase are believed to be responsible for the enhancement in strength and the formation of a reticulated structure of the Laves phase in HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 results in the improvement in ductility.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

Key components in magnetic fusion reactors, such as the divertor or the plasma-facing materials (PFMs), are required to have stringent properties including low activation, high melting point, good thermomechanical properties, low sputter erosion, and low tritium retention/codeposition. They must operate at high temperature (≥1000 K) for long durations (>10 7 s), without failure or extensive erosion while exposed to large plasma heat and an intense mixture of ionized and energetic neutral species of hydrogen isotopes (D and T), He ash (fluxes, >10 24 m −2 s −1 ), and neutrons ( [1] ). Tungsten (W) is the leading PFM candidate because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rates, and small tritium retention. These advantages are unfortunately coupled with very low fracture toughness characterized by brittle transgranular and intergranular failure regimes, which severely restrict the useful operating temperature window and also create a range of fabrication difficulties. High-damping alloys are an important family of metallic materials for applications that require noise/vibration reduction, shock absorption, and energy conversion, in structures ranging from large-scale aircrafts to small-sized electrical devices ( [1] ). Traditional alloys used to reduce noise and vibrations achieve their mechanical damping capacity by primarily manipulating crystalline defects or/and interfaces, such as dislocations ( [2] , [3] ), phase or twin boundaries ( [4] – [6] ), and magnetic domain boundaries ( [7] ). However, when exposed to mechanical vibrations and the associated stresses, both crystal defects and interfaces in these conventional alloys tend to rearrange and aggregate. As a result, the whole relaxation process is irreversible and the damping capacity gradually deteriorates ( [1] , [8] ). In addition, these irreversible relaxation processes accelerate when the service temperature increases. This means that structural stability and the high-temperature damping capacity of traditional noise reduction alloys are often insufficient for long-term use ( [8] , [9] ). High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures. Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material. frame.system: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid‐solution state with a homogeneous, single-phase microstructure.
frame.goal: To identify and verify the underlying deformation mechanism that governs the observed low hardness and strength despite good plasticity and machinability.
frame.limitation: The existing material, while displaying excellent plastic deformability and machinability, shows relatively low hardness and strength, and its deformation behavior (i.e., slip mechanisms, dislocation interactions, or possible softening dynamics) remains poorly understood.

decision.trend: Early high-entropy alloy studies first established the exceptional plasticity and machinability of equiatomic or near‐equimolar solid‐solution alloys using standard mechanical tests, but they later revealed that dislocation behavior and slip mechanisms in these materials (as in the case of the Cantor alloy studied in PMC7229066) are not fully captured by classic hardening models. Initial approaches mainly measured bulk properties, then progressed to in situ deformation studies and advanced microscopy to directly observe dislocation activities and nucleation events. However, despite this progress, fundamental questions – particularly why certain compositions (e.g., when Ti is introduced) exhibit low hardness and strength while retaining good ductility – remain unresolved.
decision.unsolved: What remains unsolved is the lack of a controlled microstructural comparison that specifically isolates the role of dislocation mobility and dynamic recovery in the as‐cast, coarse-grained, single-phase state of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi. In particular, it is unclear whether the low hardness and strength arise from an inherently low resistance to dislocation glide (possibly due to solute-dislocation interactions involving Ti) or from an inadequately activated strain hardening mechanism that could be altered by microstructure refinement.
decision.lever: Introduce grain refinement (via thermomechanical processing such as cold working followed by controlled annealing) to increase dislocation density and test for changes in strain hardening behavior while keeping composition and phase constant.
decision.why: Because past studies have gradually moved from basic mechanical measurements to in situ and advanced characterization to resolve dislocation dynamics, the logical next step is to use a controlled-variable experiment that adjusts microstructure (specifically, grain size) to directly test if the low hardness is due to facile dislocation glide or dynamic recovery. Refining the grain structure should increase the density of dislocation barriers; if the hardness improves significantly relative to the as‐cast state, it confirms that the inherent low-strength state is linked to dislocation mechanisms influenced by solute interactions (especially from Ti) and minimal internal barriers.
